Newborn Care

Hair shedding after birth and caring for your hair

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

More hair in the brush or shower after pregnancy can be unsettling. Postpartum shedding is commonly temporary, and gentle care can help with comfort and appearance while you watch for signs that deserve an assessment.

Pregnancy and birth change several hormones

Pregnancy involves substantial hormonal changes. Human chorionic gonadotropin, or hCG, is the hormone detected by pregnancy tests. Estrogen and progesterone rise during pregnancy, while prolactin and oxytocin have important roles in preparing for and supporting feeding. These hormones do different jobs; they do not all follow one simple timetable or explain every change in hair.

After the placenta is delivered, estrogen and progesterone fall sharply. Prolactin and oxytocin remain involved in lactation, with patterns influenced by feeding. It is too precise to say that every hormone returns to its pre-pregnancy level within twenty-four hours. Blood volume and circulation also change substantially during pregnancy and adjust after birth over time. Those changes provide context, but increased blood flow alone is not an established explanation for thicker pregnancy hair.

More hairs can move toward shedding at the same time

Hair follicles normally pass through growth, transition and resting phases on different schedules. During pregnancy, higher estrogen can keep more hairs in the growth phase, so less shedding may make the hair look fuller. Not everyone notices this change, and having less dramatic fullness during pregnancy does not by itself signal a problem.

After birth, more hairs may move into the resting phase and later be released. This temporary increase in shedding is called telogen effluvium. It can look dramatic because many hairs shed over a shorter period, rather than because all those follicles have been permanently lost. It is not possible to calculate it as exactly the amount “saved” during the previous nine months. Illness, blood loss, stress or other conditions can sometimes contribute as well.

The delay after birth is part of the hair cycle

The shedding often becomes noticeable a few months after delivery and commonly peaks around four months. That delay can be confusing if you expected every postpartum change to happen immediately. A fuller brush or more hair in the shower at that stage can fit the usual pattern, although timing alone does not confirm the cause.

For many people, excessive shedding eases and fullness gradually returns by the baby’s first birthday, sometimes earlier. Regrowth takes time, so the amount of hair falling and the visible fullness may improve at different rates. This is a broad expectation, not a deadline or a guarantee. Persistent thinning, a different pattern or other symptoms deserves review, and you can ask for help before a year has passed.

1. Keep styling and detangling gentle

Reduce extra breakage by avoiding excessive heat, forceful brushing and styles that pull tightly at the roots. Air drying may suit your routine, or you can use a lower heat setting when a dryer is needed. Tight ponytails, heavy extensions and repeated tension can add a separate problem to ordinary shedding. A simpler style may be easier to manage while you recover and care for a baby.

There is no universal rule that you must brush only once a day. Detangle as needed without pulling; the technique should suit your hair texture. Straight hair may be easier to comb after partly drying, while tightly curled or textured hair often benefits from gentle detangling while damp with conditioner. These steps protect hair fibres. They cannot stop follicles already moving through the postpartum shedding cycle.

2. Eat regularly and include a variety of foods

Your body needs adequate nourishment during recovery. Include protein foods, vegetables, fruit, carbohydrate and other foods that make meals satisfying. Leafy vegetables can contribute iron and other nutrients; vitamin-C-rich produce can help with absorption of plant iron. Carrots and sweet potatoes provide beta-carotene. Eggs supply protein and some vitamin D, while fish can contribute protein, omega-3 fats and minerals, depending on the type.

These are examples rather than a required hair-growth menu. A single food or a perfect daily combination cannot reverse the normal shedding cycle. If you do not eat an example food, alternatives can meet your nutritional needs. Avoid crash dieting, and ask for practical help with meals. A dietitian can support a restricted diet or difficulty eating enough, especially if recovery, illness or caring demands make regular meals hard.

3. Check supplements instead of adding more automatically

A prenatal supplement may still be appropriate after birth for some people, including during breastfeeding, but continuing the same product is not a universal hair-loss treatment. Ask your clinician which nutrients you need in your circumstances. Supplements should fill an identified or anticipated nutritional gap; they do not replace varied meals, and taking several products can unintentionally duplicate doses.

Hair gummies and high-dose biotin are often marketed for thicker hair, yet evidence for benefit without a relevant deficiency is limited. Biotin can also distort some laboratory results, including certain thyroid tests. Tell the clinician and laboratory what you take before testing. Significant blood loss or other signs of iron deficiency may warrant assessment and targeted treatment; do not start high-dose iron solely because hair is shedding.

4. Use products for appearance and manageability

A volumizing shampoo may coat hair fibres so that they look fuller. A lighter conditioner, particularly on the ends, may suit fine hair better than a heavy conditioning product that leaves it flat. Other hair textures may still need more conditioning for comfortable detangling. Choose products around your hair’s needs rather than assuming everyone should avoid conditioner.

A haircut or a different parting may also change how much thinning you notice. These are cosmetic options, not evidence that the underlying hair cycle has been treated. You do not have to buy a series of expensive products or cut your hair short if you prefer not to. Stop a product that irritates the scalp and seek advice if redness, itching or soreness persists.

Look for reasons to check beyond ordinary postpartum shedding

A clinician may consider other causes when there are distinct bald patches, a widening part, scalp inflammation, broken hairs, ongoing severe shedding or little sign of recovery. Recent fever, surgery, major stress, medications, substantial dietary restriction or blood loss can be relevant. Do not stop a prescribed medicine because you suspect it; ask for a review.

Mention tiredness that feels out of proportion, dizziness, palpitations, marked heat or cold intolerance, constipation or other new symptoms. Iron deficiency and postpartum thyroid disease are examples of conditions that may need assessment. The clinician can decide whether examination and blood tests are useful. Hormonal shedding and another treatable problem can coexist, so reassurance should fit the whole picture.

Keep loose strands away from the baby

As a practical precaution, clear shed strands from places where the baby rests or is changed. Rarely, a strand can wrap tightly around a finger, toe or another body part and restrict circulation; this is called a hair tourniquet. Unexplained swelling, redness or persistent crying is a reason to look carefully during normal care.

If a strand is loose and clearly visible, it may be possible to gently unwind it. If it is tight, embedded, difficult to see or not readily removed, get urgent medical help. Do not dig into the skin or try cutting close to a swollen finger or toe with a sharp tool. This small precaution does not mean you need to repeatedly inspect every hair you shed.

Ask for support when the change is upsetting

Hair changes can affect confidence even when the cause is temporary. You do not have to dismiss the concern because other aspects of life with a baby seem more important. Ask a clinician or dermatologist if you are uncertain about the pattern, and seek help sooner for patches, scalp symptoms or other health changes. If fullness has not returned by about a year, a review is sensible.

Before an appointment, note when shedding began, how it has changed, any birth complications, illnesses, medicines and supplements. Occasional photos in similar lighting may help if they do not increase anxiety; daily counting is not necessary. The aim is to identify the cause, support recovery and choose a manageable routine rather than promise that a particular shampoo or vitamin will stop the process.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Dermatology guidance describes increased shedding a few months after birth, often peaking around four months and improving over time.

Hair-care changes can reduce breakage or improve appearance; persistent or unusual loss needs assessment for the cause rather than automatic supplementation.

How BeMama can help

Keep the routine simple and ask for help with meals and recovery. Bring a list of medicines and supplements if you arrange a hair or general health review.

When to seek help

Seek assessment for bald patches, an inflamed scalp, persistent thinning or other symptoms such as palpitations or marked fatigue. A tight hair wrapped around a baby’s swollen finger or toe needs urgent help.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Hormonal changes can synchronise shedding after pregnancy.
  • The usual delay and recovery vary between people.
  • Gentle styling reduces extra breakage without stopping the cycle.
  • Foods and supplements are not guaranteed regrowth treatments.
  • Persistent or unusual changes deserve a clinical assessment.

Frequently asked questions

Why does shedding start months after birth?

The change in the hair cycle takes time to become visible. More hairs move into a resting phase before being released, so shedding may be most noticeable several months after delivery.

Does every hormone return to normal within twenty-four hours?

No. Estrogen and progesterone fall rapidly after placental delivery, but hormones have different patterns and lactation affects some of them. There is no single twenty-four-hour reset for the whole body.

Am I losing exactly the hair I kept during pregnancy?

That is an oversimplification. Pregnancy may reduce shedding and postpartum changes may release more hairs together, but the amount cannot be calculated as an exact nine-month backlog.

Should I brush only once a day?

There is no universal once-daily rule. Detangle gently as needed using a method suited to your hair texture, and avoid tugging, excessive heat and tight styles.

Can carrots, eggs or fish stop the shedding?

They can contribute useful nutrients as part of a varied diet, but no single food is a proven way to stop ordinary postpartum shedding. Adequate overall nutrition and assessment of a suspected deficiency matter more.

Should I keep taking prenatal vitamins for my hair?

Ask which supplement, if any, is appropriate for your postpartum and feeding needs. A prenatal product is not a treatment for hormonal shedding, and extra supplements can duplicate nutrients.

Are high-dose biotin products worthwhile?

Evidence for improving hair without a relevant deficiency is limited. Biotin can interfere with some blood tests, so tell your healthcare team and laboratory if you take it.

Can volumizing shampoo speed regrowth?

It can make hair look fuller, but that is a cosmetic effect. It does not establish faster regrowth or treatment of the underlying shedding cycle.

Do I have to wait a year before getting help?

No. Seek advice sooner if the pattern worries you, there are bald patches or scalp symptoms, or you have other health changes. Lack of recovered fullness around a year is another reason for review.

What should I do about a hair tightly wrapped around my baby’s toe?

Get urgent medical help if it is tight, embedded or not easily unwound, especially if the toe is swollen or discoloured. Do not dig into the skin or use a sharp tool close to it.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
